open_obligations: Check whether debate variants with judge interaction or abstention remain zero-sum.
Note Chen et al.'s own limitation that general-sum language games are unstudied.
Check that LLM debaters' outputs fit Chen et al.'s finite-action game model.
in.other_title: Debate modelled as a zero-sum game, so external regret minimization suffices
in.rationale: Irving et al. define debate as a zero-sum game where each agent maximises its probability of winning. Chen et al. state AI Safety via Debate is predominantly captured by zero-sum games, where coarse correlated and correlated equilibria are Nash equilibria, so the game can be played efficiently by minimising external regret.
in.scope: proposed DEPENDS_ON: modelling AI debate as a zero-sum game so that external-regret minimisation suffices

open_obligations: Check how closely Brown-Cohen et al.'s formal debate, in which both provers send a message each round and a verifier V with oracle access outputs zero or one, matches Irving et al.'s game with alternating statements and a judge.
Note that inference-time trust in A depends on B being a capable opponent.
Check how many human verifier queries training actually needs.

Note that the judge's role differs: in Irving et al.'s question-answering game a human judge sees the whole debate and decides which agent wins, while in Brown-Cohen et al. actual human raters answer only the verifier's oracle queries during training, and no human feedback is used at inference, when the model is asked to solve a problem or follow complex natural language instructions.
in.other_title: Training and inference with debate: human labels needed only for verifier queries
in.rationale: Irving et al. define debate as a zero-sum game in which each agent maximises its probability of winning. Brown-Cohen et al. define a debate, citing Irving et al., as a triple (A, B, V) of oracle Turing machines with an oracle O and a common input, in which provers A and B exchange messages over k rounds and the verifier V then outputs zero or one. Their training mapping has pretrained debaters trained by self-play to win the zero-sum game given by the debate protocol, with human labels only for verifier queries, and trusts A's output at inference unless B aborts or points out a flaw; this relies on the debate they credit to Irving et al., in their own formalisation.
in.scope: proposed DEPENDS_ON: training debaters by self-play on the zero-sum game given by a debate, which Brown-Cohen et al. define citing Irving et al., and, at inference, trusting A's output unless B aborts or points out a flaw

open_obligations: Check whether judge-ended debates preserve the zero-sum structure Irving et al. assume.
Check whether Michael et al.'s debaters are humans or AI agents.
Check that certified quotes do not make the judge's task trivially verifiable.
Note that Michael et al.'s debaters are randomly assigned to two answers, one of them correct, while Irving et al.'s agents state their own answers, which may be the same.

Note that Michael et al.'s debaters write opening statements simultaneously, without seeing each other's, and the judge sees each debater's last speech only after both are submitted, whereas Irving et al.'s agents take turns making statements s0 to s(n-1).

Note that Michael et al.'s debates concern questions about a story that the debaters quote from, whereas Irving et al.'s game is stated for a general question-answering setting with questions, answers and debate statements, and the cited passage mentions no source text.
Note that Michael et al. relax Irving et al.'s restriction that judges should automatically vote against a debater that has been caught in a lie.
in.other_title: Turn-based debate with certified quotes and judge-ended rounds
in.rationale: Michael et al. state that their approach builds on Irving et al.'s AI Safety via Debate proposal, with notable differences: they assign debaters answer choices instead of letting them choose their own, and they allow the judge to interact with the debaters between each turn. Irving et al. define a debate game where two agents state answers, alternate statements and a judge picks the winner. Michael et al. define a debate where the judge states prior credences, interjects between turns, ends the debate when ready, and debaters can include certified verbatim quotes from the story up to l_q characters per turn; these additions change the game from fixed alternation to judge-controlled interaction.
in.scope: proposed EXTENDS: two-debater debate protocols decided by a judge, extended with judge interaction and certified evidence

open_obligations: Check whether the prover-verifier game is presented anywhere else in the paper as derived from debate, or only contrasted with it here
Confirm that the robustness belief attributed to Irving et al. is stated in that paper
in.other_title: Anil et al. recast Irving et al.'s two-debater game as a one-prover game aimed at learning proof protocols
in.rationale: The authors position their game relative to Irving et al.'s debate game and state what they change (one prover instead of two debaters, and a focus on discovering proof protocols rather than on adversarial debaters lending robustness). Irving et al. define the simplest debate game, in which two agents state answers to a question, take turns making statements, and a judge decides which agent wins. Both records concern game-theoretic set-ups in which agents make statements to convince a judge, but neither bears on the other's claim: the passage only contrasts the two designs and does not say the prover-verifier game is built on debate, and the target is a definition that states no question or result for the source to answer, test, support or challenge, so the link is navigation only. The passage does not claim agreement or conflict with debate results.
in.scope: proposed SHARES_TOPIC: Game-theoretic set-ups in which one or two agents communicate statements to convince a judge or verifier; holds as a design contrast, not a comparison of results

open_obligations: Check Irving et al.'s original rule that a judge should vote against a debater caught in a lie
Note that assigning answers changes incentives relative to Irving et al.'s self-chosen answers, so equilibrium arguments may not transfer directly
Read p13 L44-52 for the authors' full reasoning on relaxing the lie rule

Check who the debaters are and how a debate ends in Michael et al., since the cited passage does not say, whereas Irving et al.'s simplest game has two agents that take turns making statements s0 to s(n-1) before the judge decides
in.other_title: Michael et al. build on Irving et al.'s debate: assigned answers, judge interaction, softer lie rule
in.rationale: The passage explicitly says the approach builds on Irving et al. and lists the changes, which is the definition of EXTENDS. The third change relaxes Irving et al.'s restriction that judges should automatically vote against a debater caught in a lie.
in.scope: proposed EXTENDS: Debate protocol design; the changes are made for information-asymmetric reading comprehension; in Michael et al. the judge interacts with the debaters between each turn to state beliefs, ask questions and make requests, whereas Irving et al.'s judge sees the debate (q, a, s) and then decides which agent wins

open_obligations: Check that the citing protocol (simultaneous arguments, fixed three rounds, 900-word limit) is described elsewhere in the paper as the operationalised variant
Check whether Irving et al.'s PSPACE-style results rely on judging a single step, which full-transcript judging would not cover
in.other_title: Khan et al. replace Irving et al.'s sub-component judging with full-transcript judging
in.rationale: The authors contrast their results with what they describe as a stricter protocol proposed by Irving et al., in which only a sub-component has to be judged to validate the entire debate, and report that judging over full debate transcripts is already useful for producing expert labels using only non-experts and untrustworthy experts. Irving et al.'s simplest debate game, the record targeted here, already has the judge see the whole debate (q, a, s); the authors study such full-transcript judging empirically, with findings that generalise to different base LLMs as debaters and judges and to human judges, which fits EXTENDS.
in.scope: proposed EXTENDS: Debate protocol design: the authors' full-transcript judging relative to Irving et al.'s simplest debate game, in which the judge sees the whole debate (q, a, s), not the stricter sub-component protocol the authors also attribute to Irving et al.; holds for LLM debaters with LLM or human judges

text: The authors define the simplest debate game: a question is shown to two agents, each states an answer (the answers may be the same), the agents alternate statements s0 to s(n-1), and the judge sees the question, answers and statements and decides which agent wins. The game is zero-sum, with each agent maximising its probability of winning.
title: Definition of the two-agent debate game (answers, alternating statements, judge)
